articles.text: One-hundred years later, the descendants of Piedmont’s first black family intend to file a lawsuit against the city seeking to rectify the loss of their property and generational wealth 100 years ago. The lawsuit was filed by the Legal Defense Fund, the nation’s first civil rights law firm, on February 2, in Alameda County Superior Court on behalf of the descendants of Sidney and Irene Dearing. The Dearings faced a sustained campaign of intimidation, including threats of lynching, cross burnings, brick-throwing, and attempted bombings. “It’s deeply painful, but necessary, to confront the trauma and other harms my family continues to face because of governmental action to take my great-grandparents’ home solely because they were Black homeowners,” said a descendant of the Dearings and plaintiff in the lawsuit. The family is asking for a remedy for the loss of generational wealth, educational access, and other resources that come with a home in Piedmont. The suit seeks damages related to the long-term value of the lost property, an official apology, and other remedies. articles.text: Editor: The proposed sculpture to reckon with a racist episode in Piedmont’s past is ugly. That is the point. Drawing red lines on a map to separate people based on the shade of their skin is brutal and ugly. The sculpture suggests those red lines that inspired the term “redlining”. It is an unsettling reminder of our past and a way to say “Never again.” –Linda Loper

articles.text: Piedmont Asian American Club will ring in the Lunar New Year with an evening of performances, food, and community celebration on Friday, February 27, at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The annual event will run from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. and will feature a traditional Lion dance, and include performances by Piedmont High School students, crafts, and a raffle. Food and drink will include dim sum, boba drinks, and panang curry, with gourmet desserts and specialty drinks provided by Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. The Lunar calendar is based on a combination of lunar and solar movements, with the second new moon after the winter solstice marking the beginning of the new year. This year, the Lunar New Year landed on Tuesday, February 17. Piedmont’s celebration will take place the following Friday. The 2026 Lunar New Year marks the year of the Horse, which is known for its energetic and dynamic nature. It symbolizes vitality, speed, and perseverance. People born in the year of the Horse are believed to possess similar traits, such as being hardworking, warm-hearted, and independent. PAAC invites all community members to celebrate the year of the Horse with them. “Come together, share joy, and honor the rich traditions of Lunar New Year with family, friends, and the vibrant spirit of our community,” said event organizer Della Chow. Tickets are limited and expected to sell out. General admission is $25 and includes dinner. Tickets may be purchased at https://bit.ly/4rlmA6K or by scanning the QR code in the poster. articles.text: This year, the City is reviving the Volunteer of the Year award for the first time since 2019. The City is also introducing a new award: Young Volunteer of the Year (under age 25), intended to uplift the meaningful contributions young people make across Piedmont. Piedmont has long been known as the “City of Volunteers.” This award, first introduced in 2014, recognizes community members whose volunteer service helped strengthen Piedmont in 2025 – whether through neighborhood improvement, arts and culture, direct community support, or building a more welcoming and inclusive community. Nominations open through March 13 To nominate a volunteer, complete the online nomination form by Friday, March 13: https://form. jotform.com/260417487348162. Volunteer service can take many forms – from a long-running commitment to a concentrated effort that made a real difference in a single year. Nominations may recognize service that strengthened Piedmont Past Winners of Piedmont’s Volunteer of the Year: 2014 – Allen “Doc” Gardner 2015 – Susan Herrick 2016 – Carla Betts 2017 – Marilyn Weber 2018 – Susan Hill 2019 – Lyman Shaffer 2025 – Stan Silverman (Police Volunteer of the Year) 2025 Police Volunteer of the Year, Stan Silverman, accepting his award next to former Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. through areas such as: • Community enrichment: improving neighborhoods and shared spaces, from beautification and clean-ups to public safety and neighborhood initiatives • Culture & Heritage: preserving local history, celebrating Piedmont’s diverse community, and supporting cultural events • Arts: strengthening the community through the visual and performing arts, arts educa- • • tion, events, and mentorship Social: direct community support and humanitarian service, including work with seniors, children, individuals with disabilities, families, and community health and safety Allyship: fostering belonging and solidarity, challenging bias, and helping make Piedmont a safe and welcoming community for everyone Nominations will be reviewed using a blind scoring process that considers measurable impact, service dedication, innovation and leadership, and character and values. Top-scoring nominees are then forwarded to a City Council subcommittee for final selection. Awardees will be recognized at the City’s annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception on April 20, 2026.

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center to celebrate splashdown Incredible advancements are made every day in the pursuit of space exploration. This year marks an especially exciting milestone in space travel with the launch of Artemis II. As early as March, the Orion spacecraft will travel around the moon and back. For this incredible mission, NASA astronaut Victor J. Glover has been selected to be the Pilot. Glover’s role in Artemis II will help pave the way for future space travel and explorers alike. The path of an astronaut Born and raised in California, Victor J. Glover attended Cal Poly where he earned a Bachelor of Science in General Engineering. While attending Cal Poly, Glover was a NCAA Division-I wrestler and football player. He also led efforts to establish the first student-funded outreach and retention center in the California Public University system. After graduating from Cal Poly in 1999, Glover joined the U.S. Navy. While serving in the Navy, Glover earned a Master of Science in Flight Test Engineering, a Master of Science in Systems Engineering, and a Master of Operational Art and Science. In the Navy, Glover was a test pilot in the F/A-18 Hornet, Super Hornet, and EA-18G Growler. Over the course of his career, Glover has garnered 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 different aircrafts, completed over 400 carrier arrested landings, and 24 combat missions. NASA astronaut Victor Glover has been selected as the Pilot of Artemis II. Out of more than 6,000 candidates, Glover was selected in 2013 to be one of eight members of the 21st NASA astronaut class. In 2018, Glover was assigned to his first spaceflight mission as Pilot of the Crew Dragon spacecraft. Glover also served as Expedition 64/65 Flight Engineer aboard the International Space Station. Glover’s extensive education and experience in science, engineering, and flying made him the perfect candidate to be selected in 2023 for Artemis II Pilot. Looking to the future Victor J. Glover is helping to lay the foundation for future space exploration and travel. The successful completion of Artemis II will send Glover and his fellow crew members into the next phase of the Artemis program: the exploration of the lunar South Pole. If the mission is successful, Glover will be the first person of color to walk on the surface of the Moon. Astronauts like Glover will help inspire generations of space explorers for years to come. Splashdown at Chabot Chabot Space & Science Center plans to host a splashdown party to celebrate this incredible achievement in space travel. This stellar event will include moonthemed crafts and snacks, special guest speakers from NASA Ames, and a livestream of the splashdown in Chabot’s planetarium, theater, and NASA Ames Visitor Center. For updates on this special event and more visit chabotspace.org. The date will be determined once a launch day has officially been selected for Artemis II, so keep an eye on our events calendar: chabotspace.org/ programs/events-listing.
articles.title: Victor Glover selected as Pilot for Artemis II

articles.text: Piedmont for Inclusive Education (PIE) will host its second annual benefit concert supporting the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Sidekicks program on February 27. The concert will feature We Are Leaves, formerly The Date Nights, a band made up of Piedmont parents, at Piedmont Community Hall from 7 to 9 p.m. The band, made up of Beach Elementary parents, describes its music as “indie pop.” Lead singer and guitarist Matthew Zapruder said the group writes “songs that have recognizable melodies and structures but are maybe a little quirkier than those you might hear in your car on the radio.” “We write songs about our local community: they mention Dracena Park and its audible owls, as well as a local ghost who lives in Dracena named Celeste,” said Zapruder. Proceeds from the concert will benefit the Sidekicks program, led by Larisa Martiniak. The program pairs neurodiverse children with a dedicated teen sidekick to help them navigate activities, build social connections and participate more fully and confidently in summer camps and other programs. Through the experience, teen sidekicks develop communication skills, patience, adaptability and emotional intelligence. We Are Leaves will play live music at the Benefit Concert, with Matthew Zapruder (left) (lead vocals and guitar), Peter Jaeschke (bass), Supina Mapon (violin and vocals), and Steve Pearson (drums). “Having older kids help neurodivergent kids in after school and other programs makes inclusion actually happen, by supporting families and kids who wouldn’t otherwise be able to participate in those activities,” said Zapruder. The Sidekicks program trains Piedmont teens to support safe, fun and inclusive after-school classes and summer programs for neurodiverse school-aged children. Last year, Sidekicks supported more than 60 Piedmont participants, and 45 teen sidekicks were trained. “The Sidekicks program has changed my kid’s life. He has so much more confidence having a buddy help him through what could easily be overwhelming experiences,” said one Piedmont parent. Sidekicks program offerings, new classes and camps, and increase staff training will be supported by the concert. Learn more about the Sidekicks program at Piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/recreation/ adaptive_programs__sidekicks To buy tickets for the Sidekicks Benefit Concert visit: Piedmontstore.org/products/ pie-piedmonters-for-inclusive-education-copy?

One could say that Anne and Greg Wheeler’s connection to Valentine’s Day started with the idea of a slow-cooked Italian meal. They met in San Francisco in 2011, while volunteering for the non-profit called Slow Food that protects traditional cooking and farming practices; the organization was founded when the first McDonald’s opened in Italy in 1986. Anne was still in a relationship when they met, so Greg, like good cooking, took things slow and built a good friendship with Anne over the next year. “Then we both stopped volunteering, and after a couple of missed opportunities to reconnect, finally — I was still trying to find my Anne — I saw her. She had just joined Match.com that day.” said Greg. “Literally that day I found her, we went out, and I just fell in love.” Greg still recalls being smitten upon finding Anne’s online dating profile, on which she included her chickens with names like Pollo Picasso, and Eggy Vedder. “I took my profile down the next day, I never even got a date out of it,” said Anne. The couple dated while living in San Francisco for a year and a half, before getting married on October 11, 2014 on Stinson Beach. Anne described the wedding as perfect, she grew up going to her family’s beach house in Stinson. A month after the wedding, Anne enrolled in a 12-month culinary school program, San Francisco Cooking School, before doing her stage at the Italian restaurant A16. “Anne was in her third trimester, with our first, standing up all day long, working in the restaurant. And I’m at home, with my head exploding, wondering, ‘when is my wife and our babyto-be, going to come home?’ She was walking backwards up a hill to get to her car, working so her husband wouldn’t starve at home,” he said with a smile. The couple lived in San Francisco’s Upper Haight district for four years, then moved to Crocker Highlands for five, before moving to Piedmont in 2022, where Anne grew up. The Wheelers started a cook book club with five other couples in 2017 upon moving to Oakland, which was a great way to reestablish their life together in the East Bay. The Wheelers have three daughters at Wildwood; Izzy is ten and their twins Millie and Bea are seven. Valentine’s Day is big in the Wheeler household, Anne is the founder of Saltysistersbakeshop.com and works overtime for a month leading up to Valentine’s Day filling cookie orders. “Valentine’s Day is our girl’s favorite holiday. Everyone makes Valentine’s for their classmates, and Izzy does very elaborate homemade Valentine’s. So we start that a month before. She made friendship bracelets one year for everyone, and then little clay statues specific for each person another year” said Anne. It’s not all Italian food and sugar cookies for the Wheelers, one of the first trips they took together was to Vietnam. There, they took three cooking classes one in the north, one in central Vietnam and then the south. “Those cooking classes, were no small affair,” remembered Greg. “Each one was about five, six hours long. You’re taken to the market, you buy all the food, bring it back, you prepare the meal, and then you get to sit down and eat it. It was amazing.” The Wheelers of Piedmont, provide the proof that the fastest way to the heart is through the stomach. Their love for one another goes beyond food however; Anne and Greg’s surely could endure hunger strikes of victuals in the name of their nuptials. Anne and Greg’s wedding picture

articles.text: Piedmont High school students Katie Tran and Anna Szymanski published their new children’s book When Ken Needs A Minute on February 4. Tran, a junior, penned the text of the book, and Szymanski, a sophomore, created the illustrations. When Ken Needs A Minute is designed to help young kids, specifically those with neurodiversities like autism spectrum disorder, to better understand their emotions. The story brings Ken the Elephant to life in 25 pages. “As students who are passionate about mental health, inclusion, and education, we wanted to create a resource that could help make a positive impact in our community and beyond,” said Tran. The duo independently published the book and copies can now be purchased at Amazon. com/When-Needs-Minute-Neurodiversity-Self-Regulation/dp/ B0GMGDBQ3C/. “We especially enjoyed collaborating throughout the creative process, as well as receiving feedback from educators, parents, and individuals who work closely with neurodivergent children. Their insights helped shape the overall direction and purpose of the book,” said Tran. The story helps children explore feelings, practice self-regulation, and celebrate individuality. When Ken Needs A Minute is marketed to parents, teachers, and therapists of children threeeight years old. A moral of the story is that being yourself and taking a minute when you need it, is always enough. articles.text: Sam Shelby (left) and Jordan Alemania, PHS Class of 2025 graduates, both committed to play at Division 1 NCAA programs. Two former football players from Piedmont High’s Class of 2025 graduating class are off to play at the next level. Last month, Sam Shelby announced he signed on to continue playing at Williams & Mary, while Jordan Alemania is set to join Holy Cross. Both players departed from Piedmont without immediately joining a college program, instead opting to take a fifth year of high school at The Hun School, a prep school in Princeton, New Jersey. They recently sign with two Division 1 NCAA programs. “It was a discussion I had with the coaches both at Piedmont and The Hun. The coaches at Piedmont knew I had what it took to play at the Division 1 level and at a good school. Coach Todd Smith at The Hun said, ‘If you come here, you’ll earn what you deserve, you just have to prove it on the field.’” Shelby said. “I heard that some older Piedmont football players from the early 2000s took some postgraduate years on the East Coast and landed at some good Division 1 programs. Coach Smith reached out to me and talked about what they had to offer,” Alemania mentioned. The Hun School put Shelby and Alemania alongside a wealth of collegiate talent and athletes who could very well be in the NFL one day. In total, 21 students from Sam and Jordan’s class have signed with D1 college programs, including the No. 1 ranked edge rusher in the entire 2026 class, USC Trojan-bound Luke Wafle. The Raiders’ program took on some of the best nation’s schools. They traveled to Orlando, Florida to play No. 2 ranked school, St. Frances Academy. They also hosted IMG Academy, which has produced hundreds of professional athletes across a wide array of sports. “To go from a smaller school like Piedmont to a program like The Hun allowed me to be around a lot of Division 1 level players and people with the same goal as me. It was really helpful to prepare for the next level, fine tune my habits, and dial into every single aspect. It was really fierce competition; we played some top- 10 schools in the nation,” Alemania said. “I’m a big believes in being the product of your environment. Up and down the roster is 40 guys that are likeminded and all have the same goals. You play alongside guys who are doing big things, you’re going to follow suit. The practice environment alone was huge,” Shelby mentioned. The pair traveled across the country to create new opportunities. “Coach Smith (at the Hun School) has been in the business a really long time. He has so many connections, especially on the East Coast. Coming to The Hun gave me geographically more exposure. On the East Coast, we’d have coaches come visit who were just a quick drive away, instead of having to fly in. It was really helpful,” “Recruiting is more difficult when you’re talking about schools that are all the way across the country. Football, especially, has less college programs overall in California compared to the East Coast. Being out there was super helpful because coaches were funneling in to see our team,” Alemania said. articles.text: An exhibition at the Legion of Honor is shedding fresh light on the artistic partnership between two leading figures of French Impressionism. Manet & Morisot, on view now through March 1, is the first major exhibition devoted to the friendship and creative exchange between Édouard Manet and Berthe Morisot, both celebrated French Impressionist artists. Spanning 15 years from 1868 to 1883, the Manet & Morisot exhibition traces the evolution of the artists’ relationship in Paris at a pivotal moment in the development of modern art. Manet is widely regarded as a pioneer of modern painting, while Morisot was the only woman to exhibit under her own name in the original Impressionist group. Their story has often centered on Manet’s early portraits of Morisot, with her work framed as an extension of his influence. However, a new scholarship presented in the exhibition challenges that narrative. By the final years of his life, curators argue, Manet increasingly followed Morisot’s lead, adopting her choice of subjects, lighter palette and rapid, expressive brushwork. Though close friends and part of the same avant-garde circles, the two artists differed markedly. Manet, known for his charm and ambition, worked primarily in the studio, revising his canvases extensively to achieve a spontaneous effect. His paintings are noted for their bold graphic power and engagement with art history. Morisot, by contrast, was admired for her reserve and intelligence. Trained largely as a plein-air painter, she developed a style defined by light, atmosphere and swift execution under shifting outdoor conditions. Her compositions often shimmer with delicacy and immediacy. Through paired works and new research, Manet & Morisot reexamines their celebrated friendship and recasts their roles in shaping modern art. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more. The exhibition leaves the museum on March 1.

articles.text: Jazz trumpeter Dave Rocha appears in concert with his trio Jazz trumpeter Dave Rocha will perform a free concert with his trio at the San Francisco Botanical Garden this Saturday, February 21. Rocha is a celebrated trumpeter who has been playing professionally for most of his adult life, having worked for years in the New York jazz scene performing alongside legendary bands of Lionel Hampton, Larry Elgart, and Machito. He also leads his own jazz combo in numerous club engagements across the United States. The concert, entitled Jazz Amongst the Magnolias, celebrates one of the most significant conservation collections of Magnolias in the United States. Magnolias bloom January through March at San Francisco Botanical Garden, offering a unique and magnificent concert background. In addition to playing the trumpet, Rocha will also perform with the flugelhorn, a cousin to the trumpet that has a deeper, more mellow tone. The concert program includes Dave Rocha compositions by Freddie Hubbard, Alan Onaje Gumbs, Ornette Coleman, Jackie McClean, McCoy Tyner and more. Guitarist Luke Schwartz and acoustic bassist Heath Proskin round out the trio. The concert begins at 1 p.m. on Saturday, February 21. No advance registration is required. Admission to the San Francisco Botanical Garden is free for all members, San Francisco residents, children under four-yearsold and military veterans. Rain cancels the event. Visit https://gggp.org/event/ jazz-amongst-the-magnolias/ to learn more.

articles.text: A new exhibition at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco highlights the bold experimentation reshaping contemporary Japanese ceramics. “New Japanese Clay” brings together modern and contemporary works that reimagine a centuries-old tradition. Infused with vivid color and sculptural ambition, the pieces range from rugged, earthbound forms that evoke stone and soil to delicate constructions that appear as light as paper or billowing fabric. Museum officials said the presentation reflects both Japan’s rich ceramic history and the increasingly global nature of contemporary art training and practice. The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters who are expanding the expressive possibilities of clay. According to Chief Curator Dr. Robert Mintz, who organized the exhibition, the featured artists build on the legacy of the mingei, or folk art, movement while forging distinctly experimental paths. “The artists in New Japanese Clay are challenging the conventions of functional ceramics and pivoting toward a purely sculptural experience,” Mintz said in a statement. “Their creations are meant to intrigue and delight; the vessel form is just a point of departure for spectacular experimentation.” Through innovative materials and techniques, the artists move beyond traditional utilitarian forms, emphasizing texture, scale and abstraction. Many also share their creative processes through social media, offering audiences insight into the technical and conceptual development behind their work. All works on view are drawn from the collection of Dr. Phyllis A. Kempner and Dr. David D. Stein. The exhibition is made possible with support from Tania and Michael Stepanian, with sustained funding provided by the Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Endowment Fund for Exhibitions and the Kao/Williams Contemporary Art Exhibitions Fund. For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/new-japanese-clay/. Discover oral care for the whole family. harmonyoralhealth.com/ scheduling (510)986-0220

articles.text: The White Elephant Sale, Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) decades-old, largest annual fundraiser, closes this weekend with an open warehouse sale. The White Elephant sale is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of over 100 year-round members, to raise proceeds to support the museum in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements and more. The White Elephant Sale is touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale and garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The fundraiser has contributed over $23 million to the Museum since the Board’s inception in 1959. The sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Volunteers sort, repair, and price items donated by the public, building a collective effort that benefits the museum and local residents alike. articles.text: Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo in Wicked: For Good The second half of Universal’s ambitious adaptation of the Broadway phenomenon Wicked arrives with greater emotional weight and sharper political edges. Where last year’s first installment reveled in the spectacle of Shiz University and the effervescence of early friendship, Wicked: For Good steps into more complicated territory: betrayal, propaganda and the cost of choosing conscience over comfort. Directed again by Jon M. Chu and based on the stage musical by Stephen Schwartz and Winnie Holzman, the film completes the story of Elphaba and Glinda as the Wizard tightens his grip on Oz and dissent becomes dangerous. Cynthia Erivo deepens her portrayal of Elphaba, now fully embracing the mantle of the so-called Wicked Witch. Erivo’s performance is less about green makeup and flying broomsticks than about moral isolation. Her Elphaba is not defiant for sport but because she sees injustice and cannot look away. The film’s most powerful moments are quiet ones, when her resolve carries a cost visible only in her eyes. Opposite her, Ariana Grande gives Glinda unexpected complexity. In the first film, Glinda’s charm and comic timing dominated. Here, Grande allows doubt and ambition to coexist. Glinda is not a villain, but she is tempted by proximity to power. The tension between the two women becomes the emotional engine of the film, culminating in scenes that feel less like fantasy spectacle and more like a breakup between best friends who have chosen different futures. The supporting cast benefits from the darker tone. Jonathan Bailey brings steadier presence to Fiyero, no longer simply a romantic foil but a man forced to confront his own loyalties. articles.text: On past walks the group had walked the length of St. James Drive to Corpus Christi Catholic Church but had never gone inside the church or considered its history. St. James is a long, flat, easy-to-walk street. Going last Wednesday to the end of the street at Park Boulevard would reward the walkers with a tour of the church. However, when the walkers gather at the Exedra, the forecast had changed. Rain was to be coming early morning, but a group of over 40 walkers showed up, hoping for the best. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, past beautiful yellow daffodils and white azaleas at the top of Piedmont Park, to Sheridan, Wildwood, and Crocker Avenues, and Hampton Road to Hampton’s meeting with St. James Drive. St. James is seven tenths of a mile long to its end at Park Blvd. The group started their walk at the two white columns that mark one of the entrances to St. James Woods, a large, 1920s real estate neighborhood development. The walkers noted a very large, uprooted tree stump on a steep slope whose tree had obviously once blocked the street after a winter storm. There were also many lovely gardens in front yards. A mature cactus garden was especially appreciated. However, as they began walking a light rain started to come down. Some walkers decided to go back after the rain started, but over 30 walkers made it to Corpus Christi’s lower driveway where Father Leo Edgerly came out to greet them. Some church history was shared. The Corpus Christi Parish was founded in 1929 as part of what was then the archdiocese of San Francisco. Reverend Francis D. Ahern was appointed pastor effective November 4, 1929. He formally opened the parish on Sunday, November 24, when he celebrated the church’s first Mass. The new parish first operated from a rented cottage at 222 St. James Drive, which doesn’t exist today. In 1930 the archdiocese purchased the property at St. James Drive and Park Boulevard for the construction of a combined church and rectory that started in September of that year. On Sunday, January 11, 1931, Archbishop Hanna blessed the new church that seated 160 parishioners and the rectory. In November 1933, Father Edwin J. Keller began his three-decade tenure as pastor of the Corpus Christi Parish. There were then 250 families in the parish and Father Keller immediately began planning for the construction of the present-day church. The new church was dedicated on Sunday, March 8, 1936. The church building is often thought to represent California Mission architecture but it is actually based on the ecclesiastical architecture of the hills in Piemonte, Italy in the 10th Century. Shortly after the church’s completion, a parishioner commissioned Ansel Adams to photograph it. The parish continued to flourish and opened the Corpus Christi School in September 1956. It has a K-8 student body and is the fourth elementary school in Piedmont. In 1962, the church was renovated and extended by 55 feet, doubling its size. It now has a seating capacity of 1,000 parishioners. Construction of a new rectory commenced in August 1966 and was completed in May 1967. In 1997, the City of Piedmont required a seismic retrofit of the church building and pastor Father Albano Oliveira developed a master plan for the church. It included the renovation and improvement of the church building, an activity building, and improvements to the school. In June 1997, the parishioners moved to the school auditorium, where masses were celebrated until December when they were able to return to the church. The finished church was dedicated on Sunday, March 29, 1998. Between June and December of 1998, the church’s Gibson Center and Plaza were constructed next to the church, completing the master plan. Father Oliveira officially opened the center on December 27. However, to everyone’s sorrow, he died unexpectedly two days later. Father Leo Edgerly was appointed pastor in 1999. Twenty-seven years ago he summarized the church’s history in a single sentence, “They sowed the seeds; we reap the benefits.” Father Leo invited the walkers to come into the church where they sat in pews as he shared information about the church. In my experience, the most difficult part of painting buildings is not finding the painting contractor, not the scraping, sanding or surface preparation, not dealing with the mess. The most difficult part is the selection of colors. Maybe this is because like most aspects of the architectural field, color selection is a curious mix of art and science, and…we A variation on the classical color wheel fashioned by Sir Isaac Newton in 1666 that we all learned in grammar school. Although modern physics reveals variants on the principles involved, they still hold true when mixing paint. Colorists continue to use the color wheel to determine harmonious color combinations. all experience colors differently. Balancing the main color attributes of hue (color: red, blue, etc.), intensity (saturation or purity), and value (lightness/ darkness i.e., tints/shades) with other associated variables is simply a difficult job. In the end, from the bold, emotion-evoking colors of Mexican architects such as the famous Luis Barragan, to the restrained, subtle colors we are most familiar with in the Bay Area, exterior colors on a building reveal, perhaps more than anything else, the attitudes, ideas and personality of the owners. Building colors should first respond to the character, style, and detailing of the architecture. Schemes with multiple colors require a natural stopping/starting point for color changes such as a different material or corners and offsets in wall planes. Certain interior colors need also be coordinated, most notably curtains and shades which are seen through the windows and have to work with the exterior colors. Because all urban buildings are surrounded by neighboring buildings, as well as landscape planting, paving, and other elements, exterior color selection necessarily also involves urban design considerations; each building is part of a larger neighborhood palate. Evaluation of color requires certain steps to be successful. Most importantly, although not nearly done often enough, is to allow enough time for color selection and approval before painting starts. Once an attitude and concept is settled upon, selection begins with little paint chips – only the first step. Many architectural offices specify that large (100 sf) samples then be painted on at least two different walls of the building with different natural light conditions. These must be allowed to dry for at least a few days before being evaluated. It is good for owners to then reflect on the samples at different times of the day for a good week before modifications are made or final approval given. A fine example of a more “calm” color scheme that prioritizes, works with, and enhances the surrounding landscaping. Using somewhat similar colors, these two homes, after creative responses to the different architecture detailing, result in a very different feeling – both terrific! Many times, it is difficult to describe exactly why a color scheme is so attractive. But the important thing is to simply recognize it as good, and to know that you like it.

articles.text: Is your furry friend feeling a little off? Diarrhea and vomiting are common stressors for pet owners because our beloved canine companions tend to explore the world with their mouths. Digestive problems can be challenging for both dogs and their owners, but a few tips and tricks on what to feed and when can go a long way. First, it can help your dog a great deal if you withhold food for a couple hours after they have had an episode of vomiting or diarrhea. This allows the stomach to stabilize. Make sure plenty of water is available if the dog is thirsty, as digestive issues are often accompanied by dehydration. For dogs with mild stomach issues, veterinarians often recommend a “bland diet.” Many owners have heard this term but are unaware of the wide range of options on it. Rice is a classic soothing food; it is easy on the stomach and can help firm up stool. Boiled chicken breast is another great option, providing lean protein that’s gentle on the digestive system. Many owners will combine chicken and rice for a few days until symptoms improve. But these aren’t the only options. Scrambled eggs (with no seasoning) are also a good choice, offering another easily digestible protein source. Further, plain pasta is a simple carb dogs can enjoy which is easy on the tummy. To add some extra hydration or to tempt a dog who finds their very plain diet unappetizing, consider adding low-sodium chicken broth. A tablespoon or two of plain Greek yogurt can also go a long way, providing probiotics to support gut health. If your dog is particularly ill, feed these new band diet options in small freScooter the Great Dane checks out his bowl, eager to feel better on the bland diet. quent meals to ease digestion. Although not strictly on the bland diet, adding some plain canned pumpkin to your pup’s food can assist with necessary fiber to ease digestion. This is a good option for dogs who have ongoing issues with stool that is too firm or too soft, but who are not sick. If your dog has a pre-existing health condition, such as kidney disease, it is crucial to consult with your veterinarian before making any changes to their diet. These dogs may require a special diet, such as restricted protein, and sudden changes can be harmful. For dogs on prescription diet, it is often best to continue this diet to avoid tummy upset from sudden changes. If your dog’s symptoms persist or worsen after a couple days on the bland diet, consult with your vet to rule out underlying issues. With a little patience and the right foods, your pup should be back to their playful self in no time. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. articles.text: Frederic Vignobles On a sunny afternoon in the Pacific Northwest, the ferry ride from Seattle to Bainbridge Island offers stunning views of the snowcapped Olympic mountains to the west and majestic Mount Ranier to the southeast. The crossing of the Puget Sound takes about a half hour, and it’s a short walk to the quaint main street. After perusing the local bookstore and small shops, one can stop in the downtown tasting room that pours some of the wines of the Eagle Harbor Wine Co. For a richer experience we recommend making the short drive to the winery located on what used to be a Christmas tree farm. It’s in a contemporary light industrial building adjacent to a distillery, a sculptor’s gallery, and the Bainbridge Island’s artist cooperative known as BARN. Most days, you can taste a full range of wines, tour the facility, and often have the chance to speak with the folks making the wine. Eagle Harbor Wine Co. is owned and operated by Emily Parsons, who grew up drinking European wines. Like many of us, she embraces the “wine is food” and “good wine is part of a good life” philosophy. Unlike most of us, she went on mid-career to pursue studies through UC Davis, apprentice with founding Eagle Harbor winemaker Hugh Remash, and, a dozen years ago, purchasing the winery outright. Her vision was to meld the high-quality fruit grown in eastern Washington with carefully selected oak barrels from single forests in France and a minimalist approach to winemaking that respects the intrinsic qualities of the grapes. pages.text: 24 24 Wednesday, February 18, 2026 Pawsitive relief: A guide to the bland diet for dogs with digestive issues By Sierra Berrick Is your furry friend feeling a little off? Diarrhea and vomiting are common stressors for pet owners because our beloved canine companions tend to explore the world with their mouths. Digestive problems can be challenging for both dogs and their owners, but a few tips and tricks on what to feed and when can go a long way. First, it can help your dog a great deal if you withhold food for a couple hours after they have had an episode of vomiting or diarrhea. This allows the stomach to stabilize. Make sure plenty of water is available if the dog is thirsty, as digestive issues are often accompanied by dehydration. For dogs with mild stomach issues, veterinarians often recommend a “bland diet.” Many owners have heard this term but are unaware of the wide range of options on it. Rice is a classic soothing food; it is easy on the stomach and can help firm up stool. Boiled chicken breast is another great option, providing lean protein that’s gentle on the digestive system. Many owners will combine chicken and rice for a few days until symptoms improve. But these aren’t the only options. Scrambled eggs (with no seasoning) are also a good choice, offering another easily digestible protein source. Further, plain pasta is a simple carb dogs can enjoy which is easy on the tummy. To add some extra hydration or to tempt a dog who finds their very plain diet unappetizing, consider adding low-sodium chicken broth. A tablespoon or two of plain Greek yogurt can also go a long way, providing probiotics to support gut health. If your dog is particularly ill, feed these new band diet options in small freScooter the Great Dane checks out his bowl, eager to feel better on the bland diet. quent meals to ease digestion. Although not strictly on the bland diet, adding some plain canned pumpkin to your pup’s food can assist with necessary fiber to ease digestion. This is a good option for dogs who have ongoing issues with stool that is too firm or too soft, but who are not sick. If your dog has a pre-existing health condition, such as kidney disease, it is crucial to consult with your veterinarian before making any changes to their diet. These dogs may require a special diet, such as restricted protein, and sudden changes can be harmful. For dogs on prescription diet, it is often best to continue this diet to avoid tummy upset from sudden changes. If your dog’s symptoms persist or worsen after a couple days on the bland diet, consult with your vet to rule out underlying issues. articles.text: Last month I wrote about my friend Jackie. This is part two of her story, still unfolding in real time. I wish I could tell tell you everything turned out smoothly. I can’t. Like many life transitions, this one has been layered, emotional and far more complicated than anyone expected. After years of thinking about it, Jackie made the move to Merrill Gardens. Leaving her home of 35 years was no small decision, but the stairs had become too much. I constantly worried about her falling. She lived alone and rarely had visitors. Something had to change. Still, choosing a senior community meant more than a new address. It meant being surrounded by people after a lifetime of independence and solitude. Jackie is a bit of a loner, so this was going to take adjustment. The move itself was stressful, but the real hurdle came after the boxes arrived. Unpacking became overwhelming. Finding a place for everything felt impossible to her, and she would not accept help. Not even putting away a single plate, because then she “wouldn’t know where it was.” A plate. A stapler. Toilet paper. Five months later, she still isn’t settled. Both her financial planner, who had recently moved his own mother, and I offered professional organizers. She refused. Pride, fear, control. It’s rarely just one thing. Then, about a month ago, Jackie fell. She landed in the emergency room. After a short stay, she was sent back to her apartment, though it was clear she couldn’t safely manage on her own. Getting to the bathroom, managing medications, arranging meals. All of it was too much. Somehow, she ended up back in the ER again. I’m still unclear on the details, but it seemed like the only way to trigger the next level of care. Kaiser transferred her to an assisted living facility, where she remained mostly bedridden. I’m her friend, not family or an official advocate, but I could see things weren’t right. I asked a nurse about physical therapy. “She’s getting it daily,” they told me. Jackie said she wasn’t. That disconnect became the norm. “That’s not true,” she’d say. It became hard to know what was accurate and what wasn’t. Jackie has since returned to her independent living community, but she is no longer independent. She needs assistance now. And this is where we are today: facing the reality of care needs, resistance to help, and the very real concern about cost. We plan for college. We plan vacations. We make lists for holiday meals. But do we truly plan for aging? For the day errands become exhausting. When driving feels unsafe? When managing medications gets confusing? Ask yourself: • Will I keep my car? • How will I get to the bank? • Who will pick up prescriptions? • How will I get to doctor’s appointments? • Who will help with taxes, bills, laundry and meals? • Do loved ones know my passwords and how to access medical information? • The list goes on. Tasks that once felt simple can quickly become overwhelming. Often, these transitions happen suddenly. A fall. An illness. A moment that changes everything. Please start the conversation now, while you’re healthy and clear-minded. It’s one of the greatest gifts you can give your family and yourself. A lifetime of memories, belongings and decisions doesn’t sort itself out in a crisis. Just as we use professionals to plan travel or manage finances, there are caregivers, advocates, organizers and senior service experts ready to help with this stage of life. Planning is the key to making an emotional transition as smooth as possible. It’s never too early to begin. And one day, you’ll be grateful you did. This is part two of her story, still unfolding in real time. I wish I could tell tell you everything turned out smoothly. I can’t. Like many life transitions, this one has been layered, emotional and far more complicated than anyone expected. After years of thinking about it, Jackie made the move to Merrill Gardens. Leaving her home of 35 years was no small decision, but the stairs had become too much. I constantly worried about her falling. She lived alone and rarely had visitors. Something had to change. Still, choosing a senior community meant more than a new address. It meant being surrounded by people after a lifetime of independence and solitude. Jackie is a bit of a loner, so this was going to take adjustment. The move itself was stressful, but the real hurdle came after the boxes arrived. Unpacking became overwhelming. Finding a place for everything felt impossible to her, and she would not accept help. Not even putting away a single plate, because then she “wouldn’t know where it was.” A plate. A stapler. Toilet paper. Five months later, she still isn’t settled. Both her financial planner, who had recently moved his own mother, and I offered professional organizers. She refused. Pride, When is it time to stop living independently? fear, control. It’s rarely just one thing. Then, about a month ago, Jackie fell. She landed in the emergency room. After a short stay, she was sent back to her apartment, though it was clear she couldn’t safely manage on her own. Getting to the bathroom, managing medications, arranging meals. All of it was too much. Somehow, she ended up back in the ER again. I’m still unclear on the details, but it seemed like the only way to trigger the next level of care. Kaiser transferred her to an assisted living facility, where she remained mostly bedridden. I’m her friend, not family or an official advocate, but I could see things weren’t right. I asked a nurse about physical therapy. “She’s getting it daily,” they told me. Jackie said she wasn’t. That disconnect became the norm. “That’s not true,” she’d say. It became hard to know what was accurate and what wasn’t. Jackie has since returned to her independent living community, but she is no longer independent. She needs assistance now. And this is where we are today: facing the reality of care needs, resistance to help, and the very real concern about cost. We plan for college. We plan vacations. We make lists for holiday meals. But do we truly plan for aging? For the day errands become exhausting. When driving feels unsafe? When managing medications gets confusing? Ask yourself: • Will I keep my car? • How will I get to the bank? • Who will pick up prescriptions? • How will I get to doctor’s appointments? • Who will help with taxes, bills, laundry and meals? • Do loved ones know my passwords and how to access medical information? • The list goes on. Tasks that once felt simple can quickly become overwhelming. Often, these transitions happen suddenly. A fall. An illness. A moment that changes everything. Please start the conversation now, while you’re healthy and clear-minded. It’s one of the greatest gifts you can give your family and yourself. A lifetime of memories, belongings and decisions doesn’t sort itself out in a crisis. Just as we use professionals to plan travel or manage finances, there are caregivers, advocates, organizers and senior service experts ready to help with this stage of life. Planning is the key to making an emotional transition as smooth as possible. It’s never too early to begin. And one day, you’ll be grateful you did.
